definition.text: A game, also called the assurance game or trust dilemma, in which players do best by cooperating on an ambitious goal but can fall back on a safer solo option that protects them if the other does not cooperate.

facts.text: Two hunters choose separately whether to hunt a stag, which needs both of them, or a hare, which one can catch alone but is worth far less.
It has two pure equilibria: hunting stag together pays most, while hunting hare alone is the safer, risk-dominant choice.
Unlike the prisoner's dilemma, mutual cooperation is itself an equilibrium; what it needs is trust.
It is often used as an analogy for social cooperation such as international agreements on climate change.
The problem originated with Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Discourse on Inequality; David Hume gave examples such as two neighbours draining a meadow.
Orcas that cooperatively herd fish to the surface, which needs many orcas, are an animal example.
Expected punishment of defectors can turn a prisoner's dilemma into a stag hunt.

definition.text: One strategy dominates another if it always gives a better result, whatever the other players do.

facts.text: Strict dominance means always strictly better; weak dominance means never worse and sometimes better.
A strategy that dominates every alternative is a dominant strategy; rational players are usually assumed never to play dominated strategies.
If every player has a strictly dominant strategy, the game has a single dominant-strategy equilibrium, which need not be good for everyone.
The prisoner's dilemma is the classic case: confessing dominates for each suspect although both would do better staying silent.
Strictly dominated strategies are never part of a Nash equilibrium, but weakly dominated ones can be.

definition.text: A way of solving games by repeatedly crossing out dominated strategies until no more can be removed.

facts.text: Removing some strategies can make others dominated in the smaller game, so the step is repeated.
It relies on rationality being common knowledge: everyone knows that everyone knows, and so on, that all players are rational.
With weakly dominated strategies the result can depend on the order in which they are removed.

definition.text: A player's complete plan for a game, saying what they will do in every situation that might arise.

facts.text: A move or action is any one of the options a player can choose where the best result depends on what others do as well.
A strategy is like a list of directions, and a move is a single step on that list.
A player's strategy set lists every strategy available to them, such as {rock, paper, scissors}.
In games played over time or with private information, strategies are rules for how to respond to each possible history or piece of information.
Choosing the strategy sets well is part of the art of making an applied game both solvable and meaningful.

definition.text: A strategy in which the player chooses among their pure strategies at random with set probabilities, rather than committing to one plan.

facts.text: A pure strategy is a fully fixed plan; it counts as a mixed strategy that picks one option with probability 1.
Mixing helps where no pure strategy is a best response, keeping a player unpredictable; payoffs are then expected payoffs.
A soccer penalty kick has no pure-strategy equilibrium, so kicker and goalie should both randomize their direction.
Not every finite game has a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium, as matching pennies shows, but every one has an equilibrium once mixing is allowed.

Critics in the 1980s found mixed strategies intuitively problematic; Harsanyi's purification reads them as our ignorance of players' private information, and another view treats them as shares of a population.

definition.text: A strategy that randomizes separately at each information set over the actions available there, rather than over whole plans.

facts.text: A mixed strategy randomly picks a fixed path through the game tree, while a behavior strategy takes a random path.
Kuhn's theorem shows the two are equivalent in finite extensive-form games with perfect recall, where players remember all past actions.
The Absent-Minded Driver game shows why perfect recall is needed for this equivalence.
